panels.visual_direction: FULL-BLEED HORIZONTAL PANORAMA. Two armies face each other across a wide, dust-choked plain at the foot of the Tahsing Hills. The Yellow Turban forces mass on the left: a ragged sea of yellow banners, roughly-armored peasant soldiers, and rebel cavalry. On the right: a smaller, grimly ordered imperial column, their banners crisp against the haze. Center foreground: three riders advance slightly ahead of the imperial line — Liu Pei, composed and still, both swords sheathed at his hip; Chang Fei to his left, eighteen-foot serpent-spear already leveled, his war-horse straining forward like a loosed arrow; Kuan Yu to his right, the Black Dragon blade resting across his saddle, his long beard lifting in the wind. The hills loom in Song Dynasty ink-wash style behind both armies — vast, indifferent, ancient. The sky is a flat white-gold haze. Dust catches the light in sweeping diagonal arcs. The scale is mythic: tiny human figures against geological eternity. The emotional register is the held breath before a thunderclap.
dialogue: Liu Pei: Sons of Han — your quarrel is with those who have failed you, not with the people who bore you! Lay down your yellow banners. Yield now, and Heaven will forgive what men cannot!
Chêng Yüan-chih: Silence that man. Têng Mou — ride out and answer him in blood!
panels.narration: The rebel host of the Yellow Turbans massed at the foot of the Tahsing Hills like a tide that had forgotten how to recede — their hair flying loose about their shoulders, their foreheads bound with yellow cloth, their banners a ragged sea against the white-gold haze of the sky. Against them rode Liu Yüan-tê with his two sworn brothers, one on each side, as they had solemnly promised before Heaven and Earth beneath the flowering peach trees: united in aim, united in heart, united unto death, or not at all. Yüan-tê raised his whip and his voice carried across the dusty plain with the authority of the Han blood in his veins, calling upon the rebels to throw down their weapons and surrender. Their leader, full of rage, did not answer with words.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT VERTICAL PANEL, LOW ANGLE — almost ground-level. Chang Fei at full gallop, seen from below and ahead. His war-horse is a blur of motion, hooves barely grazing the earth, ink-streak speed lines radiating from every edge of the panel. Chang Fei’s face is a mask of absolute ferocious focus — not rage, but the cold certainty of a man who has already seen the end of this moment. The eighteen-foot spear extends before him like a strike of lightning, the iron tip catching the pale sky. Rebel officer Teng Mou, visible in the upper right corner, is turning his horse in panic — too late. His expression: the moment a man understands he has already lost. The spear tip is aimed dead center at his chest. Diagonal composition — everything angles toward the point of impact. Heavy ink-wash shadows on Chang Fei’s armor; Teng Mou half-dissolved in the harsh backlighting.
panels.narration: At once rode forward Chang Fei, his long spear poised to strike — eighteen feet of iron-tipped certainty, forged from a thousand catties of the finest steel in the days when the world still seemed a thing that could be set right. Têng Mou had ridden out to silence Yüan-tê; he had not yet understood the difference between a man full of fury and a man who has already seen the end of the moment. Chang Fei did not shout a war cry. He simply came.

panels.visual_direction: CLOSE-UP IMPACT PANEL — brutal geometry, almost abstract. The spear tip has erupted through the center of Teng Mou’s chest armor from the front. He arches violently backward off his horse, body forming a sharp backward arc — the classic shuǐmò figure of a man surrendering to physics. Blood radiates in ink-splash patterns, not gory but stylized — like a calligrapher’s deliberate brushstroke, as if the universe itself is recording the moment. The spear shaft fills the panel diagonally. Chang Fei’s gauntleted fist on the shaft is all we see of him — anonymous, instrumental, inevitable. Teng Mou’s face: not pain but pure astonishment. His yellow turban, knocked free, spirals off-frame. Deep chiaroscuro: the wound-point is the only bright spot in the panel, everything else pooled in shadow.
panels.narration: One thrust, and Têng Mou rolled from his horse, pierced through the heart. He had ridden out to begin the battle; instead he ended his own part in it, which is a different kind of ending entirely. For one long, suspended moment, ten thousand men stood in perfect silence and watched the space where their champion had been — and in that silence the morning shifted beneath their feet, and the world became a slightly different shape.

panels.visual_direction: HALF-PAGE VERTICAL — the dominant image of the spread. Kuan Yu and the rebel leader in single combat, resolved in a single stroke. Kuan Yu is captured mid-swing — the Black Dragon blade a sweeping diagonal slash that bisects the entire panel from upper-left to lower-right. The rebel leader is already divided: the geometry of the cut is clean, almost architectural, the two halves of the figure separating with terrible symmetry. This is rendered not as gore but as classical tragedy — the broken line of a man who chose the wrong side of history. Kuan Yu himself is monumental: long beard horizontal in the wind of his own stroke, eyes half-lidded with the calm of absolute mastery. His red war-cloak billows behind him like a battle standard. The horse beneath him hasn’t even broken stride. Background: swirling battlefield smoke rendered in loose ink-wash, impressionistic. The scale of Kuan Yu against the chaos makes him seem carved from different material than the world around him — stone among water.
dialogue: Chêng Yüan-chih: I will not be shamed by a single rider — I will cut you all down myself!
Kuan Yu: Then come.
panels.narration: Chêng Yüan-chih, full of rage at the death of his man, whipped his own steed forward with sword raised, riding to slay Chang Fei himself. But Kuan Yün-chʿang — he of the phoenix eyes and the silkworm brows, whose whole appearance was dignified and awe-inspiring — had already swung up the great curved blade he called Cold Beauty, that ponderous weapon of a full hundredweight, and rode to meet him. At the sight of that man upon that horse with that sword, fear seized upon Chêng before he could recover himself, and ere he could do so the great sword fell, cutting him in halves. One stroke. The histories would argue about many things. Not this.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE HORIZONTAL PANEL — aftermath. The battle is over in the same moment it began. Yellow Turban soldiers flee in every direction, their banners fallen, horses riderless. Chang Fei and Kuan Yu rein in their horses at the center of the battlefield, facing each other across a field of dust and scattered yellow cloth. Between them and slightly behind: Liu Pei on his pale horse, both swords still at his hip — they were never drawn. He watches his brothers with an expression of profound, complicated love: pride threaded through with the first faint shadow of something heavier. He alone seems to understand the weight of what just happened. The Tahsing Hills rise behind all three of them, vast and ancient. The light has gone golden — late afternoon or the particular gold of moments that become legend. The composition echoes a classical Chinese court painting triptych: each man separate, each complete, each diminished without the others.
dialogue: Chang Fei: Elder brother — one thrust! Did Heaven itself not smile upon us today?
Kuan Yu: The man was brave enough to ride out. He chose a poor morning for it.
Liu Pei: Two new swords… and they needed neither of mine. Heaven has been more generous than our oath deserved.
panels.narration: Their leader fallen, the rebels threw away their weapons and fled, and the official soldiers dashed in among them; many thousands surrendered before the sun had moved a hand’s breadth across the sky, and the victory was complete. Three brothers who had sworn brotherhood and unity of aims beneath the flowering peach trees stood now at the center of a broken army — and the eldest of them, Liu Yüan-tê, had never once drawn his swords. He watched his brothers across that golden field and felt the full, complicated weight of what it meant to have chosen well.

panels.visual_direction: NARROW VERTICAL GUTTER PANEL — the full height of the page, barely two inches wide. A single ink-brush detail: the severed yellow turban of the rebel leader, lying in the dust. A thin line of dark ink pools beneath it. In the far background, barely suggested by three or four brushstrokes, the retreating dust cloud of a broken army. Nothing else. The negative space — the white of the page — is the real subject. This is the panel that breathes. The poem caption runs vertically down the right margin, styled as classical Chinese verse lettering.
panels.narration: When the dust settled, the historians set aside their plain accounting and reached for a different instrument. Some victories refuse prose — they demand to be sung, the way a sword demands a worthy hand. Two heroes new to war’s alarms rode boldly forth to try their arms; their doughty deeds three kingdoms tell, and poets sing how these befell.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Chang Pao's Black Magic — Phantom Armies from the Storm
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages in a two-act structure. Page One (Act One — The Summoning): Panel 1 is a wide horizontal establishing shot spanning the full page width at top. Panels 2 and 3 sit side by side below it — Panel 2 a tall vertical close-up, Panel 3 a wide horizontal. Page Two (Act Two — The Unraveling): Panel 4 opens as a full-width horizontal. Panel 5 is a large vertical panel dominating the lower left, with Panel 6 a smaller square inset at the lower right — a quiet visual resolution after the storm. The ink-wash style should treat the storm panels with loose, gestural brushwork bleeding into the gutters, while the final panel returns to controlled, spare linework to signal the return of earthly order.

panels.visual_direction: Full-width establishing shot. Wide low-angle view looking up at Chang Pao on horseback against a sky in violent transformation. He is silhouetted from below, a lone figure atop a rearing warhorse, his long hair unbound and whipping horizontally in a wind that has no earthly source. His sword arm is raised straight overhead, blade pointing at the heavens like a lightning rod. Above him, the sky is a churning ink-wash catastrophe — black and grey clouds boiling and spiraling inward as if the sky itself is being drawn into a drain. The horizon behind him still holds pale light, making the darkness above him feel localized, intentional, summoned. Use extreme contrast: the horse and rider rendered in hard muscular linework against backgrounds that dissolve into atmospheric wash. Motion streaks of wind rake across the panel horizontally. The composition echoes a classical Chinese scroll — the tiny human figure commanding something vast and terrible.
panels.narration: The rebel Chang Pao, while still mounted, loosened his hair, grasped his sword, and gave voice to his incantations. The sky above the battlefield darkened as though a curtain were being drawn across the heavens — not the slow grey dimming of any natural storm, but something sudden and deliberate, as if an unseen hand were willing the darkness into being. The wind rose from nothing, howling across the hills with a sound no earthly gale had ever made. Thunder answered his raised blade like a soldier obeying his lord.

panels.visual_direction: Tight vertical close-up: Chang Pao's face from the chest up, hair streaming wildly in every direction like black ink dropped in water. His eyes are wide, whites showing, lips moving in incantation — not a villainous snarl but something more unsettling, the focused trance of a man who genuinely commands forces beyond himself. His sword hand is raised at the panel edge. Behind him, the cloud mass is now so close it seems to press against his back, thick with churning darkness. A single crack of lightning bleaches one side of his face white, leaving the other in absolute shadow. Dramatic chiaroscuro rendering — this is the soul of the scene. The ink-wash background should feel like it is physically pressing against the figure.
panels.narration: This was the art Chang Pao had mastered in the mountain passes where the Yellow Heaven sect kept its forbidden texts — word and will and steel raised together toward the sky. His lips shaped syllables that belonged to no dynasty, no court, no common tongue, older than the empire he sought to break. A crack of lightning bleached one side of his face white and left the other in absolute shadow, as though the storm itself were already claiming half of him for its own terrible purpose.

panels.visual_direction: Wide horizontal shot — the descent of the phantom army. The black cloud mass fills the upper two-thirds of the panel, and from within it, ghostly cavalry and infantry materialize in downward diagonal streaks. They are not fully solid — rendered in loose, smeared ink-wash strokes that suggest horses, lances, banners, faces screaming without sound — recognizable as soldiers but translucent, made of storm. Below, Liu Pei's troops are caught in full rout: men throwing down weapons, horses bolting, formations collapsing in every direction. The diagonal lines of the phantom descent contrast violently with the horizontal scatter of the fleeing men. Use explosive compositional energy — diagonal ink streaks, motion blur. A few soldiers look directly up in frozen terror, faces rendered in precise, heartbreaking detail against the chaos around them. The scale should be overwhelming — thousands above, thousands below, one man's will made into catastrophe.
dialogue: Fall back! Fall back — there is no fighting what the sword cannot touch!
panels.narration: Within the dense black cloud were horse and footmen innumerable, and they swept downward to attack the imperial troops — not fully men, not fully spirit, but something that wore the shape of both and the mercy of neither. Fear came upon Yüan-tê's soldiers as it comes upon all living things when confronted with proof that the world holds more than they had ever believed. They did not flee in cowardice: they fled in the oldest wisdom of the body, the knowledge passed down from the first battles of men, that courage is no shield against what cannot die.

panels.visual_direction: Full-width horizontal shot from above, looking down from the clifftop perspective — the counter-strike. Along the ridge of rocky cliffs above the battlefield, rows of hidden soldiers are revealed, heaving great clay urns and wooden buckets over the edge. The contents cascade downward in dark streams — blood from slaughtered swine, goats, and dogs — falling in long arcing lines toward the phantom army below. The soldiers on the cliff are rendered in solid, earthy linework, fully real and physical, a deliberate visual contrast to the ghostly translucence below. Their faces are grim but purposeful. One figure — Chu Chien — stands at the cliff edge pointing downward, commanding the pour. Below, the streams of blood and filth are just beginning to intersect with the swirling phantom mass. A single moment suspended before dissolution.
dialogue: He uses magic — his phantom hosts are conjured from the storm itself.

Then we shall answer with what the spirit world cannot abide. To-morrow I shall prepare counter magic: the blood of slaughtered swine and goats and dogs. This blood shall be sprinkled upon their hosts from the precipices above by men whom they see not. Thus shall we break the power of their black art.
panels.narration: Chu Chien had deliberated through the night, and he had remembered what the old texts said: that the dark arts cannot endure the blood of base creatures, that what the spirit world exalts may be undone by the earth's most common and unclean things. He had spent the hours of darkness in grim preparation — great clay urns of the blood of swine and goats and dogs carried without torches to the high cliffs by men who moved in silence. Now the two younger brothers, each commanding a company, crouched hidden upon the heights with a plentiful supply of filth, and waited.

panels.visual_direction: Large vertical panel — the dissolution of the phantom army, the visual climax of the scene. The phantom cavalry and infantry are mid-air, caught in the precise moment of unmaking. Where the cascading blood touches them, the ghostly forms are literally shredding apart — figures that were soldiers become ragged strips and fragments, exactly like wet paper torn by rain. Use extraordinary ink-wash technique here: tight controlled linework for the fragments closest to the viewer, dissolving into loose gestural wash as they scatter upward and outward. The transformation is simultaneous across hundreds of phantom figures — a cascade of dissolution from the top of the panel downward. The black storm-clouds are visibly retreating, thinning, the darkness pulling back. In the lower portion of the panel, real rebel soldiers are suddenly exposed where the phantoms stood — confused, unshielded, the magic stripped away. Their faces show the specific terror of men whose weapon has just vanished.
panels.narration: The masses of men and horses in the air fluttered to the earth as fragments of torn paper — and this was the precise and terrible word for it, paper, as though the whole dread host had been nothing but an inkbrush lie written across the face of the sky. The wind ceased to blow. The thunder subsided. The sand sank and the pebbles lay still upon the ground, as though the world itself exhaled in the long aftermath of the sorcerer's undoing. Where the phantom armies had stood, there were now only rebels — mortal men, stripped of their borrowed darkness, blinking into the pale and returning light.

panels.visual_direction: Smaller square panel — a moment of stillness and resolution. Wide shot of the battlefield from a middle distance. The sky above is clearing, the last tatters of black cloud pulling apart to reveal pale, exhausted light. On the ground, scraps of what was the phantom army lie scattered like debris after a storm — indistinguishable now from fallen leaves or torn paper. In the middle distance, Liu Pei's brothers are already charging forward on horseback into the exposed rebel lines, their banners snapping forward in the direction of attack. Chang Pao's horse is rearing back in the far distance, the sorcerer himself diminished, small against a sky that no longer belongs to him. Use very spare, deliberate brushwork — the visual chaos of the previous panels resolves into controlled Song Dynasty landscape simplicity. Negative space dominates the sky. The composition should feel like the final line of a poem: quiet, exact, final.
dialogue: His sorcery is spent — they are men and nothing more! Forward — charge!
panels.narration: Chang Pao quickly saw that his magic had been countered and turned to retire — but there was no road of retreat left open to him now. On his flanks came Kuan Yü and Chang Fei with their companies, swift as hawks dropping from the hillside; in his rear came Yüan-tê and Chu Chien, closing the last avenue of escape. The rebels were routed, scattered like the phantom soldiers they had so recently commanded, and the sky above the field cleared to pale and indifferent light, returning at last to the world of ordinary men.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Tsao Tsao Appears — The Wolf Under Crimson Banners
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: a commanding full-width establishing shot at top (Panel 1), then two equal panels below (Panels 2 & 3). Page two: a massive half-page close-up dominating the top (Panel 4), with two smaller panels side by side beneath (Panels 5 & 6). The crimson banners should bleed into the gutter between pages, visually unifying the spread. Heavy ink-wash shadows, loose smoldering backgrounds contrast with the rigid, precise linework on Tsao Tsao and his troops. Negative space is used aggressively around Tsao Tsao to give him gravitational weight amid the chaos.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH ESTABLISHING SHOT — a smoke-choked dawn battlefield seen from a low angle, looking across a smoldering field of broken Yellow Turban soldiers in retreat. They run toward the viewer in desperate diagonal streaks of motion-blur ink. But the entire upper half of the panel is BLOCKED by a solid line of armored cavalry under enormous crimson banners, the fabric catching an unseen wind, snapping like flames. The banners fill the sky. At the dead center of the line, motionless on horseback amid all this movement, is a single figure: TSAO TSAO. He is rendered in crisp, controlled linework — every other element is loose and frantic. The contrast should feel like a stone wall meeting a flood. Lighting: fire-orange glow from the left (Huangfu's retreating conflagration), cold grey dawn from the right. The visual grammar is a Song Dynasty battle scroll cut through with a cinematic wide lens.
panels.narration: Huangfu Sung had ordered every man to cut a bundle of dry grass, and at the second watch they had set the rebel encampment ablaze — the flames rising to the very heavens, the Yellow Turbans thrown into great confusion, no time to saddle horses or don armour. The battle had continued till dawn and the rebels now fled in all directions, scattered across the smoldering plain like sparrows before the hawk. Chang Liang and Chang Pao, with their few flying soldiers, believed at last they had found a way of escape. They had not yet seen what the morning held in store for them.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — a knot of fleeing Yellow Turban rebels, faces streaked with ash and terror, skidding to a halt as they realize what is in front of them. One points, mouth open in a silent cry. Another grabs a companion's sleeve. Their yellow headbands are torn and bloodied. The background behind them is pure white ink-wash smoke. The moment of realization — escape has become a cage. Frame them from slightly above to emphasize their smallness and entrapment.
dialogue: The road — the road is blocked!
Crimson banners — those are the Emperor's men!
We have run all night only to fall into a trap!
panels.narration: Suddenly, out of the pale drift of smoke, a troop of soldiers bearing crimson banners appeared to oppose them — and every road of escape that had seemed to open now closed like a fist. They had fled from Huangfu Sung's fire in darkness and believed the worst was behind them; they had not reckoned on the soldier who had been sent precisely to catch what the fire did not consume. One man pointed, and could not find his voice. Another clutched a companion's sleeve and the two of them stood as if rooted to the cold earth.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM WIDE SHOT — Tsao Tsao's cavalry line advances at a slow, measured walk. No screaming charge — just the inexorable forward press of disciplined soldiers. The crimson banners advance with them. In the foreground, a soldier's spear tip catches the orange dawn light. Tsao Tsao himself is partially visible at mid-frame, his posture relaxed on horseback, one hand resting loose on the reins. His expression is invisible at this distance — but his stillness amid the advancing line is more menacing than any war cry. The composition echoes a classical Chinese court painting — order imposed upon chaos with bureaucratic calm.
dialogue: Tsao Tsao: Forward. Hold the line. No one leaves this field.
Officer: My lord — their formation is broken. They cannot stand.
Tsao Tsao: Then we need not hurry.
panels.narration: He had been given command of five thousand horse and foot and sent to help fight at Yingchuan, and he had arrived precisely in time to close the trap. When he was twenty he had hung clubs at the four city gates he governed, and any breach of the law met its punishment whatever the rank of the offender — even the uncle of a great eunuch had been beaten in the street for the crime of carrying a sword by night, and thereafter no one dared to offend, and the name of Tsao Tsao became terrible. Order, he had always understood, required nothing more than will, and the absolute refusal to hesitate. He walked his cavalry forward at a measured pace, unhurried, as though the rebels before him were already names inscribed in the register of the dead.

panels.visual_direction: MASSIVE HALF-PAGE CLOSE-UP — Tsao Tsao's face, rendered in meticulous, muscular ink linework. He is middle-aged but sharp: medium-length beard, small eyes that carry extraordinary calculating intelligence, a mouth set in the faintest suggestion of a smile — not cruelty, something colder than cruelty: satisfaction. The dawn light carves his face from the left in dramatic chiaroscuro, leaving his right side in deep shadow. Two crimson banner poles frame the edges of the panel like the wings of some great bird behind him. Smoke drifts across the lower quarter of his face like a veil being drawn aside. This is a face being introduced to history — and it knows it. The linework around his eyes should be the most precise and deliberate on the entire page.
dialogue: Tsao Tsao: What manner of man am I?
The Seer: You are able enough to rule the world.
The Seer: But wicked enough to disturb it.
Tsao Tsao: [quietly, still smiling] Good.
panels.narration: A seer of Junan had once looked upon this face across a table and fallen into long silence, as though the answer required great care to carry safely. Others had spoken of him in the same breath as destiny itself: rebellion is at hand, they said, and only a man of the greatest ability can succeed in restoring tranquillity — and that man is yourself. The dynasty of Han is about to fall; he who can restore peace is this man, and only he. When the seer at last gave his verdict, Tsao Tsao had received it not as warning but as gift, and he had greatly rejoiced.

panels.visual_direction: FLASHBACK INSET PANEL — small, bordered in a thin double line to signal memory. A younger Tsao Tsao lies on a mat, body convulsing in a theatrical fit, while his uncle rushes from the room in a panic. Young Tsao Tsao's eye — just one, visible above his flailing arm — is calm, watching. The style shifts slightly: looser brushwork, lighter ink wash, the dream-logic of recollection. A single candle throws long shadows. This is the boy who learned that the world could be managed if you were willing to manage it.
dialogue: Father: Your uncle said you were taken by a fit — are you recovered?
Young Tsao Tsao: I have never suffered from fits or any such illness.
Young Tsao Tsao: But it seems I have lost my uncle's affection. And it seems, Father, that he has deceived you.
panels.narration: As a young man he had been fond of hunting and delighted in songs and dancing, resourceful and full of guile, and his uncle had gone often to his father to report his misdeeds. But the youth was equal to every occasion. One day, seeing his uncle approach along the courtyard path, he had flung himself to the ground in a pretended fit — and one eye, just barely visible above the crook of his elbow, watched with perfect calm as the uncle fled in alarm to raise the father. When the father arrived, the boy stood in complete health, and the uncle's word was never trusted in that household again. Thereafter the young man grew up licentious and uncontrolled — and blissfully unobserved.

panels.visual_direction: RETURN TO BATTLEFIELD — a wide low shot looking up at Tsao Tsao on horseback against the sky, the crimson banners now fully backlit by the rising sun so they glow like burning silk. He has raised one arm — not a dramatic gesture, just a quiet, precise signal to advance. His soldiers move. The Yellow Turbans crumple before them, reduced to small dark shapes at the bottom of the frame. Tsao Tsao himself occupies the upper third of the panel: monumental, deliberate, the fulcrum around which history is turning. The ink-wash sky behind the banners bleeds from deep orange at the horizon to cold, indifferent white at the top of the frame. Below his portrait-still figure, written as a caption in the manner of a classical historical annotation:
dialogue: Tsao Tsao: Cut them to pieces. Take the banners, the horses, the drums.
Officer: My lord — the two rebel lords have escaped the field.
Tsao Tsao: Then after I speak with Huangfu Sung, I will go in pursuit of them myself.
panels.narration: "Able enough to rule the world. Wicked enough to disturb it." The seer had offered those words as a caution; Tsao Tsao had worn them ever since like armor, bright and unapologetic beneath the sun. Thousands were slain at Yingchuan and endless banners and drums and horses were taken, and not a little money besides. Chang Liang and Chang Pao slipped through his net that day, and so — with one arm raised quietly against the burning silk of the sky, a gesture as calm and final as a brushstroke closing a character — he turned his crimson columns and rode in pursuit. A hero comes; he gains renown — already destined for a crown.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Liu Pei Saves Tung Cho — And Receives Contempt
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page 1: Panel 1 is a full-width horizontal splash (top third of page) — the charge into battle. Panels 2 and 3 split the lower two-thirds as equal vertical columns. Page 2: Panel 4 is a wide horizontal establishing shot of Tung Cho's tent interior (top half). Panels 5 and 6 split the bottom half — Panel 5 a tight close-up, Panel 6 a medium shot. Use heavy ink-wash negative space between panels to evoke scroll-painting separation. The diagonal motion of battle panels should contrast sharply with the rigid, static geometry of Tung Cho's command scene.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH HORIZONTAL SPLASH. Extreme low angle looking up at three horsemen erupting from the left edge of the panel in a thunderous diagonal charge. Liu Pei leads at center, his twin swords raised, face set in fierce determination. Kuan Yu is to his right, Green Dragon halberd sweeping in a wide arc that sends rebel soldiers sprawling. Chang Fei is a black blur on the far right, his spear driving through the chaos like a lance of lightning. Behind them, Tung Cho's routed soldiers are in disarray — broken standards, fallen horses, men fleeing into ink-wash fog. The rebel Yellow Turban forces of Chang Chio scatter in the middle-ground. Motion-blur ink streaks radiate from the three brothers like brushstrokes of heaven. Dramatic chiaroscuro: a rent in the storm clouds above throws a column of harsh light down on the three brothers alone, leaving the carnage around them in deep shadow. The feeling is mythic intervention — three men reshaping the shape of a battle.
panels.narration: Two days from the road they had turned upon, they heard the thunder of battle behind some hills — and hastening to the top they beheld the government soldiers suffering great loss, the countryside thick with Yellow Turbans whose banners blazoned the words 'Celestial Duke' writ large. Yuän-tê wasted no word on counsel. 'We will attack this Chang Chio,' he said, and the three brothers spurred down from the heights into a battle already lost. Chang Chio was in hot pursuit of the broken imperial forces when they dashed into his army, threw his ranks into confusion, and drove him back — and what ten thousand soldiers of the empire could not manage, three men without rank or commission managed in a single, furious charge.

panels.visual_direction: VERTICAL PANEL, left column. Medium shot from behind Chang Chio, looking out at the battlefield from his command position on a low ridge. He is a tall, gaunt figure — robes the color of storm clouds, a yellow headband bright as a wound across his brow. His hands are raised mid-incantation, but they are lowering, the magic faltering. His silhouette is rigid with the shock of reversal. Before him, his Yellow Turban forces are breaking apart like a river striking three boulders — the three brothers visible in the far distance as small, luminous figures carving through the press. Sparse ink-wash landscape behind him: bare hills, smoke rising, the suggestion of ten thousand fleeing men rendered in loose gestural brushwork. The mood is a general watching his certainty dissolve.
panels.narration: Chang Chio had worsted Tung Cho and was following up his advantage — the field was his, the imperial banner broken, the day as good as won. He had summoned wind and thunder to his bidding; he had filled the sky with the shapes of horsemen innumerable and driven whole armies before the force of his sorcery alone. But the men who now fell upon his flank answered to no court and no heaven he had learned to bargain with, and when they dashed into the heart of his ranks and threw his army into confusion, even the Celestial Duke discovered that he had run out of incantations.

panels.visual_direction: VERTICAL PANEL, right column. A tight medium shot: the three brothers have reined their horses around Tung Cho, who sits heavily on his own mount — his armor disarrayed, his face flushed with the shame of a man pulled from the jaws of defeat. He is large, physically imposing, with a thick neck and heavy-lidded eyes that already carry contempt even in rescue. Liu Pei, Kuan Yu, and Chang Fei form a loose semicircle around him, their horses heaving, all three of them blood-streaked and battle-bright. Chang Fei's eyes burn like coals; Kuan Yu's long beard is swept back from the wind of the charge, his expression carved from composure. Liu Pei looks at Tung Cho steadily — not with hunger for praise, but with the quiet readiness of a man who already suspects what is coming. The background is the dissipating chaos of the battlefield settling into an eerie stillness.
panels.narration: Then they returned with the rescued general to his camp — all three of them blood-streaked and battle-bright, their horses still heaving from the charge that had turned the day. Tung Cho was a man born in the west at Lin-t'ao, arrogant and overbearing since youth; he had survived the afternoon not by his own arm but by the arms of strangers, and this was already a thing his pride was working to forget. He looked the three brothers over in the settling dust — the way a man of rank examines men of none — and his face spoke everything his mouth had not yet troubled itself to say.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE HORIZONTAL PANEL spanning the full top half of page 2. Interior of Tung Cho's command tent. Heavy fabric walls hung with maps and a wolf-pelt standard. Tung Cho has settled himself onto a carved command chair at center — the posture of a man who has already reclaimed authority over the situation, legs spread, one hand resting on his knee with lazy ownership. He looks the three brothers over the way a merchant examines inferior goods. Liu Pei, Kuan Yu, and Chang Fei stand before him — still in full battle gear, wounds unattended, sweat and blood on their faces. The contrast is total and deliberate: the three heroes fill the left side of the panel with hard-won dignity; Tung Cho's bloated ease fills the right. The tent lighting is from braziers below, casting upward shadows on Tung Cho's face that make him sinister without caricature — the honest face of power that needs no mask. Ink-wash technique: Tung Cho rendered in heavy, blunt linework; the three brothers in leaner, more precise strokes.
dialogue: What officers have you?
None, my lord. We are men of the land — Liu Pei of Chuo county, and my sworn brothers Kuan Yu and Chang Fei. We heard the battle and came.
Men of the land. No commission. No rank.
panels.narration: When Tung Cho had leisure to speak with the three brothers — when he had settled himself upon his command chair and reclaimed, by posture alone, the authority that Chang Chio had nearly stripped from him — his first question was not of their valor, nor of the price paid in blood to drive the rebels back. He was a man who measured all things by rank and commission, by seals of office and warrants from the capital, and for men who held none of these there was, in the architecture of his world, simply no place at all.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP, bottom-left panel. Tung Cho's face filling almost the entire frame — the gesture of dismissal caught in a single, devastating image. His hand is raised, wrist slack, the wave of a man shooing away a fly. His expression is not cruel — it is worse than cruel. It is bored. Heavy-lidded eyes already drifting away, the slight downward curl of a lip. This is a man to whom these three have ceased to exist the moment their rank was announced. Behind him, barely visible, the ghost of the wolf-pelt standard. The ink technique here uses deliberate bluntness — thick, dismissive strokes that mirror his contempt. In the lower corner of the frame, barely visible: the edge of Chang Fei's white-knuckled fist.
dialogue: Then you are nothing to me. I keep no company with men of no rank and no name.
Go.
panels.narration: The dismissal fell like a stone and spread no further. He did not send them away in anger, which would at least have been a form of recognition — he sent them away with the flat, final indifference of a man to whom they had already ceased to exist. Tung Cho turned his heavy gaze elsewhere, and the three who had ridden into a losing battle and turned it by the force of their own bodies were, in his accounting, as though they had never been. Yuän-tê retired calmly, as he withdrew from all such things — his fury swallowed whole, his eyes already fixed on a distance Tung Cho could not see.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT, bottom-right panel. Outside the tent entrance, the three brothers stand in the harsh late-afternoon light. This is the scene's heart. Chang Fei has turned — his face is volcanic, a vein standing in his neck, teeth bared, one hand white-knuckled on his spear shaft and the other arm already pulling back toward the tent. He is three seconds from action. Kuan Yu stands slightly apart, arms folded, his face a mask of cold fury held rigidly in check — the composed exterior barely containing what burns beneath. But the panel's true focal point is Liu Pei's hand on Chang Fei's forearm. It is not a gripping hand — it is a resting hand. Quiet. Certain. His face is turned toward Chang Fei, and his expression is the most complex image in the scene: there is grief in it, and fury swallowed whole, and the exhausted, deliberate patience of a man who is already thinking ten years forward. The ink is sparse here — wide negative space around the three figures, the suggestion of a vast and indifferent sky above them rendered in diluted wash. Their isolation is total. Their bond is the only architecture in the frame.
dialogue: We have just rescued this menial in a bloody fight — and now he is rude to us! Nothing but his death can slake my anger! Let me go back in there!
Remember, Fei — he holds the government commission. Who are we to judge and slay?
Bitter! Bitter it is to bow before such a wretch! I would rather slay him and be done with it. You may stay here if you wish — I will seek some other place!
We three are one in life and in death, brother. There is no parting for us. We will all go hence — together.
panels.narration: As it was in olden time, so it is to-day — the simple wight may merit well, yet officialdom holds sway. Chang Fei, the blunt and hasty, would have washed the insult out in blood then and there, and who among ten thousand men could call him wrong? But his elder brothers understood what fury could not: that the bond between three men sworn in a garden was the only thing in this world worth preserving, and that to carry that bond through a world built on contempt was the most demanding form of valor any of them would ever be asked to practice.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Liu Pei Finds His Master in a Cage-Cart
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: Panel 1 is a full-width establishing shot spanning the top third. Panels 2 and 3 split the middle row equally. Panel 4 bleeds to the bottom edge — tall and narrow, like a hanging scroll. Page two: Panel 5 is wide and low, a cinematic horizontal strip. Panel 6 is a near-full-page close composition with deliberate negative space in the ink-wash sky above — the emptiness as expressive as the figures below. Gutters are thin and dark, reinforcing confinement. The cage-cart bars should visually echo across panels as a recurring motif, fragmenting characters the way corruption fragments justice.

panels.visual_direction: Wide establishing shot — a desolate imperial road cuts diagonally through a dust-pale landscape under a bruised, overcast sky. The horizon is low, pressing the heavy clouds down. In the middle distance, an imperial escort of six soldiers marches with spears upright, their lacquered armor dull in the flat light. At the center of the column, a rough-hewn cage-cart of dark timber rolls on iron-rimmed wheels. Through its bars, barely visible, a bearded figure sits erect. Liu Pei, Kuan Yu, and Chang Fei have halted their horses on the road ahead, silhouetted against the grey sky — three dark shapes frozen in recognition. Ink-wash brushwork gives the landscape a Song Dynasty scroll quality: spare, atmospheric, vast. The road stretches ahead into nothing.
panels.narration: Halfway along the road to reinforce their teacher, the three brothers drew their horses to a halt. An imperial escort marched toward them through the pale dust — spears erect, lacquered armor dull in the flat and failing light — and at the column’s heart, rolling on iron-rimmed wheels, a cage-cart bore its prisoner toward the capital. When they drew near enough to see through the bars, the man inside was no other than the man they had ridden so far to help. The road stretched ahead into nothing, and the sky pressed down like a judgment already rendered.

panels.visual_direction: Medium close-up — Liu Pei has dismounted. He stands at the side of the cage-cart, one hand raised and gripping a wooden bar. His face is tilted upward toward the figure inside, expression cracked open with grief he is trying to master — jaw tight, eyes bright with unshed tears. His riding robes are dusty. The bars cast shadow-stripes across his face, as though he too is imprisoned. Behind him, a soldier's spear haft is visible at the panel edge — a reminder of the armed escort. Chiaroscuro lighting: harsh sidelight from the left, deep shadow on the right half of Liu Pei's face.
dialogue: LIU PEI: Teacher— I did not know. We heard nothing of this.
LIU PEI: What has been done to you?
panels.narration: Liu Pei was from his horse before it had stopped moving, his feet finding the road, his hands finding the bars of the cage. The rough timber was cold against his palms. He had not understood, until this moment, how much he had trusted that the world still contained justice — that a man who fought the rebels faithfully would be rewarded, or at the very least not punished for his virtue. The bars divided his teacher’s face into fragments, and Liu Pei could not look away.

panels.visual_direction: Inside the cage — intimate close-up on Lu Chih's face seen through the bars, the bars rendered as thick ink strokes that bisect the panel itself. Lu Chih is composed, almost serene, though his wrists bear the marks of chains. His beard is unkempt, his court robes torn at the shoulder, but his eyes are steady and clear — the eyes of a man who chose correctly and knows it. He looks down at Liu Pei with something between sorrow and paternal calm. Loose ink-wash background inside the cart: just shadow and splinter-textured wood. His dignity is the only light in the panel.
dialogue: LU CHIH: Do not grieve for me, Liu Pei. I had the means to prevent this — and I chose not to use them.
LU CHIH: There are men who can be bought. I am not one of them. I knew the price when I refused.
panels.narration: Lu Chih looked down at him with the steadiness of a man who has already made his reckoning and found it sufficient. His wrists bore the marks of chains; his court robes were torn at the shoulder; his beard spoke of days on the road and nights in the dark of the cage. But his eyes were clear as still water — the eyes of a man who had examined his choices in the silence and found no shame in any of them.

panels.visual_direction: Tall narrow vertical panel — a hanging-scroll composition. Lu Chih speaks through the bars, one chained hand raised slightly in a gesture of explanation, not supplication. Liu Pei stands below him, head bowed slightly to receive the words. The bars run vertically the full height of the panel, turning the image into something that resembles a calligraphy scroll divided by brushstrokes. Imperial soldiers are blurred suggestion in the background — present, watching, irrelevant to this private grief. The framing emphasizes the vertical distance between teacher and student, the cage elevating Lu Chih even as it degrades him.
dialogue: LU CHIH: I had surrounded the rebels and was on the point of smashing them. Then the Court sent a eunuch to enquire into my failure.
LU CHIH: He demanded a bribe. I asked him — where, in such circumstances, was I to find a gift for him?
LU CHIH: He went away in wrath. He told the Court I was hiding behind my ramparts, that I disheartened my men, that I would not give battle.
LU CHIH: So I was superseded by one Tung Cho — and now I am brought to the capital to answer for crimes that are his.
panels.narration: The story came out in measured, unhurried words — the kind a man rehearses in the dark of his cage until he has stripped them of their bitterness and left only the bare truth. Lu Chih did not rail against his fate; he set it forth with the patience of a teacher explaining a problem his students must come to understand. A man had refused to be corrupted, and the empire had taken its revenge. These were not separate events — they were the same event, and its name was the age they lived in.

panels.visual_direction: Wide low-angle horizontal strip — the three brothers in the foreground, backs partly to us, facing the cart. Chang Fei dominates the left: enormous, coiled, his white-knuckled fists strangling his spear shaft, tears cutting clean lines through the road-grime on his fierce, tattooed face. He is vibrating with violent intent, leaning forward. Kuan Yu stands right, separated by deliberate negative space — jaw set, eyes distant, staring past the cart toward the horizon as though looking at a future already decided. Between them, Liu Pei stands very still, one hand still on the bar, the other raised slightly toward Chang Fei in restraint. The cart and its escort are mid-ground. The sky above them all is ink-washed emptiness.
dialogue: CHANG FEI: Then we free him! Now! These soldiers are nothing — a handful of strokes and it is done!
CHANG FEI: I will slay the escort and break these bars myself — who dares say otherwise?
LIU PEI: No.
KUAN YU: Chang Fei. Be still, and hear him.
panels.narration: The story put Chang Fei into a rage — immediate and total, the way fire is when given air. He was for slaying the escort and setting free the prisoner without another moment’s deliberation; his body had already made the decision before his voice had finished shaping it. The soldiers were nothing to him. The law was nothing to him. There was only the man in the cage and the cowards who had put him there, and his hand upon his spear was already composing its answer.

panels.visual_direction: Near-full-page final panel — pull back to a three-quarter view. Liu Pei faces Chang Fei directly, hand on his brother's arm, his expression carrying the terrible weight of the words he is about to say. Chang Fei stares back, tears still wet on his face, fists still clenched — but he is listening. Kuan Yu has turned, watching Liu Pei. In the background, Lu Chih watches through the bars in silence, his expression unreadable but present — a witness to the lesson his imprisonment is teaching. The cage-cart has begun to move again; a soldier's boot is visible at the lower edge, the procession resuming. The top quarter of the panel is pure ink-wash sky: cloud, emptiness, the weight of heaven saying nothing. This is the scroll painting that could hang on a wall — three men learning the cost of virtue from the man who is paying it.
dialogue: LIU PEI: The Government will take the proper course.
CHANG FEI: The government put him in that cage!
LIU PEI: You must not act hastily, brother. We are men under commission — not outlaws. Not yet.
CHANG FEI: (low, through clenched teeth) Then what are we, if we walk away from this?
LIU PEI: We are men who do not add to the disorder. That is what he taught us.
panels.narration: Liu Pei looked at his brother — at the tears on that fierce face, the strangled fists, the grief that had nowhere righteous to go — and he spoke the words that cost him more than Chang Fei could know. He believed them. He had to believe them. A man who ceased to trust that justice would eventually prevail had only force remaining, and force without righteousness was the very affliction they had taken up arms to cure. In the background, through the bars, Lu Chih said nothing — and his silence, too, was a kind of instruction.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: Panel 1 is a wide cinematic establishing shot spanning the full page width — Chang Fei on horseback, a horizontal explosion of motion. Below it, two equal panels side by side: the weeping elders (left) and the inspector enthroned on his dais (right), creating visual contrast between the powerless and the corrupt. Page two: Panel 4 is a tall vertical half-page — Chang Fei's fist closing on the inspector's topknot, the moment of reversal, rendered with maximum dramatic weight. Panels 5 and 6 share the lower half: Panel 5 (wider) shows the thrashing at the post; Panel 6 (narrower, almost portrait) shows Liu Pei's departure — quiet, sword sheathed, back turned. The ink-wash treatment should grow increasingly loose and explosive through the thrashing sequence, then settle into stillness for the final panel.

panels.visual_direction: Full-width cinematic panel. Low angle, looking up from street level. Chang Fei bursts through the yamen gate on a massive dark horse, its nostrils flared, hooves scattering cobblestones like shrapnel. Two doorkeepers cartwheel away on either side — one loses his hat mid-air, one clutches a broken pike. Chang Fei is half-standing in his stirrups, eyes blood-red and blazing with wine-fury, his topknot loosened, one massive hand already raised. Motion-blur ink streaks slash diagonally across the panel. The gate's lacquered pillars crack behind him. Ink wash is wild and explosive here — the background dissolves into turbulent brushstrokes suggesting the world itself recoiling.
panels.narration: Chang Fei had been all day drowning his sorrow in wine and had drunk far too much. He called for his horse and rode out past the lodging of the inspector — and what he found at the gate stopped him as cold as a drawn blade. His eyes opened till they became circles. He ground his teeth. Then, in a single moment, he was off his steed.

panels.visual_direction: Left panel of a two-panel row. Tight, intimate shot at ground level. Three white-haired village elders huddle outside the gate, robes dusty, faces streaked with tears and the red marks of blows. One presses his forehead to the earth. Another has his hands raised in supplication toward the gate, fingers trembling. The ink wash here is sparse and heartbreaking — maximum negative white space around the figures, as though grief has consumed everything else. Their faces are rendered with meticulous, anguished linework: every wrinkle a record of endurance.
dialogue: The inspector has compelled our magistrate’s own underlings to bear false witness against him...
We came to beg mercy for Lord Liu, but we are not permitted to enter. And we have been beaten by the doorkeepers for daring to try.
Noble Sir... save us.
panels.narration: They were white-haired men, old enough to have endured much — yet here they wept like children outside a gate they were not permitted to cross, their faces still bearing the red marks of blows. They had come to plead for a magistrate who had never wronged the people to the value of a single stalk of stubble, a man who had fought in some score of battles and received this small post as his entire reward. Chang Fei looked at their trembling hands and their foreheads in the dust, and asked no more questions.

panels.visual_direction: Right panel of the two-panel row, matching height with Panel 2. Interior: the inspector sits high on his official dais, robes immaculate, face arranged in the smug composure of a man accustomed to impunity. He is surrounded by cowering clerks bearing false documents. Behind him, a painted screen depicts a tiger — ironic, given what is about to arrive. The lighting is rich and oppressive: warm lamplight from above makes him look gilded, untouchable. He is mid-gesture, hand lazily extended to receive a bribe. Then — in the extreme right edge of the panel, just breaching the frame — Chang Fei's silhouette fills the doorway like a thundercloud.
dialogue: Magistrate Liu — what was your origin?
You lie about your descent and your statement of services is false. The Court has ordered the reduction of your sort of low-class officials.
Let the record show the magistrate finds no complaint among the people...
panels.narration: The inspector had taken his seat on the dais and left Liu Pei standing below for a long time before deigning to speak. Three times already he had driven Liu Pei from his own door; now he forced the minor officials to bear false witness with their hands in bonds at his feet. He sat in his lamplight like a man who believed himself untouchable — and he was, until the silhouette filled his doorway and the warm air shifted with the cold draft of fury.

panels.visual_direction: Tall vertical half-page panel — the pivot of the entire sequence. Extreme close-up: Chang Fei's enormous fist has closed completely around the inspector's elaborately oiled topknot. The inspector is mid-air, yanked bodily from his dais, his body a diagonal slash of flailing silk robes across the panel. His face is a masterwork of shock — eyes white, mouth a perfect O, all dignity annihilated in a single instant. Chang Fei's face occupies the upper third: wine-flushed, jaw set, eyes carrying no cruelty — only the cold clarity of a man performing a necessary duty. The composition echoes a classical Chinese tiger-pouncing-on-prey painting. Ink is dense and muscular here — heavy blacks, the inspector's robes rendered with wild, panicked brushstrokes.
dialogue: Oppressor of the people — robber! Do you know me?
panels.narration: The wine was still in his blood, but the fury in his eyes was perfectly clear — it had a shape and a name, and the name was justice. Chang Fei had forced his way past the terrified doorkeepers into the rear apartments and seen the inspector sitting on high, the official underlings in bonds at his feet. He did not debate, did not threaten, did not wait. One moment the man sat enthroned in silk and self-regard; the next he was swinging in the air, hauled bodily down by the oiled topknot he had dressed with such official care that very morning.

panels.visual_direction: Wide panel, lower half of page two. Exterior courtyard: the inspector is lashed to the hitching post, robes torn, the official seal of his rank now hung humiliatingly around his own neck like a placard. Chang Fei stands slightly behind and to the left, mid-swing with a long willow switch — the switch is rendered in mid-arc, already beginning to fracture from the force. The white-haired village elders stand to the right of the panel, watching. Their expressions are not triumphant — they are the faces of people who have wept so long they are not sure how to stop. One old man covers his mouth with both hands. Another bows his head. The ink wash in the background opens wide: a pale, empty sky, the yamen walls just suggested. The inspector's broken posture against the post is rendered with merciless detail.
dialogue: If we do not beat this sort of wretch to death — what may we expect?
Noble Sir — save me! Save me!
Brother. Release him. Let him go.
panels.narration: Chang Fei lashed him firmly to the hitching post and broke a switch from a willow tree and gave his victim a severe thrashing, staying his hand only when the switch grew too short to strike with. The white-haired elders stood and watched — not with triumph, but with the quiet exhaustion of people who have spent all their tears on a single wrong and have nothing left but the witnessing of it. It was into this scene that Liu Pei stepped from the magistracy, drawn outside by shouting before his door — and he saw at once who the unhappy victim was, and asked the reason.

panels.visual_direction: Narrow vertical portrait panel — the quiet after the storm. Exterior gate, late afternoon light, long shadows. Liu Pei walks away from us, already through the gate, his figure small against a vast ink-wash sky that bleeds from pale gold to deep grey at the top. His sword is sheathed. He does not look back. His posture carries no triumph — only the straight-backed weariness of a man who knows this moment will cost him everything and chose it anyway. In the blurred background: Chang Fei follows, the broken willow switch still in his hand, his fury spent. The inspector remains visible at the hitching post, very small, irrelevant now. The ink wash here is its most restrained — sparse, deliberate, elegiac. The scene breathes.
dialogue: Brother — after your magnificent services you have only this petty post, and even here you have been insulted by this fellow. A thorn bush is no place for a phoenix. Let us leave here and go home — till we can evolve a bigger scheme.
If I hear that you injure the people, I will assuredly kill you. I now spare your life and return to you the seal.
We are going.
panels.narration: Yüän-tê had always been kindly and gracious — it was his nature as much as his politics. He contented himself with hanging the official seal about the inspector's neck and speaking his final word quietly, as a man who has already decided and requires no audience for it. Liu Pei walked into the road and did not look back. Some doors, once opened, do not close — and he understood, with the straight-backed weariness of a man who has lost and chosen at once, that the road ahead was longer and darker and more necessary than the one behind.

panel_scripts.scene_title: The Fatal Indecision of Ho Chin
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: three panels of descending width — an expansive wide shot for Panel 1, a medium two-shot for Panel 2, and a claustrophobic close-up for Panel 3. The room should visibly shrink between panels, achieved by tightening the frame and lowering the ceiling beams in the background. Page two: Panel 4 is a tall narrow vertical strip on the left margin (Chen Lin's memorial scroll); Panels 5 and 6 split the remaining page, with Panel 5 a tight face study and Panel 6 a full-width, bird's-eye establishing shot bleeding off the bottom edge. Ink-wash brushwork should grow more agitated and loose as urgency escalates — the final panel reverts to sparse, cold stillness.

panels.visual_direction: Wide horizontal shot of Ho Chin's council chamber — a vast, high-ceilinged hall of lacquered pillars and silk hangings, rendered with loose atmospheric ink-wash for the background and sharp precise linework for figures. Ho Chin sits center-frame on a cushioned dais, robes rich and layered, his posture relaxed to the point of indolence, one ringed hand resting on his knee. Yuan Shao stands before him in full battle armor, breastplate catching the lamplight, leaning forward with the coiled urgency of a man fighting gravity. Three or four advisors flank the edges, watching. The composition emphasizes the absurd contrast: a warrior tensed for action, a lord comfortable in stillness. Chiaroscuro light pours from hanging oil lamps, throwing deep shadows behind the pillars — the darkness at the room's edges feels inhabited.
dialogue: Yuan Shao: Chang Jang and Tuan Kuei are spreading word outside that you caused the death of the late Empress Dowager — that you aim at the throne itself.
Yuan Shao: Remember how Tou Wu missed his chance because the secret leaked. The conditions are now favorable. This is a heaven-sent opportunity — it will not come again.
Ho Chin: You are bold for a man whose sword has not yet left its scabbard in this matter.
Yuan Shao: The eunuchs hold the palace, the Emperor, and your sister's ear. Slay them — root and branch — or they will ruin you.
panels.narration: He had come from nothing — a butcher's son whom fortune had raised to the highest command in all the Han empire, and the years of easy power had made him a man who mistook hesitation for wisdom. Yuan Shao had laid before him a heaven-sent opportunity: the eunuchs Chang Jang and Tuan Kuei were already spreading treasonous rumors abroad, handing Ho Chin the very pretext he needed to destroy them cleanly and at once. Every advisor in that lamplit hall knew it. And so, it must be said, did every shadow gathered behind the pillars at the room's far edge.

panels.visual_direction: Medium two-shot, camera lower now — we are at Ho Chin's eye level as he sits, making the seated man appear almost equal in stature to the standing Yuan Shao. Ho Chin's soft, be-ringed hand is raised, palm outward, the gesture of dismissal. His expression is not angry — it is worse: gently condescending, the look of a man who believes he is being patient with inferiors. Yuan Shao's jaw is tight, his armored fist clenched at his side, but his eyes are not angry either — they are afraid. In the background, the ornate wall hangings seem to press inward slightly. A detail: one silk panel behind Ho Chin depicts a phoenix — noble, doomed, and beautiful.
dialogue: Ho Chin: She will not consent. What can be done?
Yuan Shao: Call up an army and slay them — it is imperative. Never mind her consent!
Ho Chin: The Empress Dowager speaks plain sense. They are old servants. To kill old servants so soon after their master's death would appear disrespectful to the Dynasty.
Ho Chin: A gaoler would be ample force. Why throw the empire into confusion over palace servants?
panels.narration: He had gone to his sister and she had argued with the patient certainty of a woman who holds the seal of the Empress Dowager: the eunuchs were old servants, she said, and to put them to death in the wake of their master's passing would dishonor the Dynasty itself. As Ho was of a vacillating mind, he had murmured assent and left her. His brother, too, had whispered the same counsel in his ear — sweetened, though Ho Chin did not know it, by the eunuchs' gifts. Now Yuan Shao stood before him in armor and demanded a plain answer, and Ho Chin gave him the one thing that came most naturally: a reason to wait.

panels.visual_direction: Tight medium shot on Tsao Tsao standing alone before Ho Chin — no armor, no retinue, just the man himself in plain court robes, composed and terrifyingly still. His eyes are level and cold, reading Ho Chin the way a surgeon reads a wound. Ho Chin is partially cropped out of frame, only his cushioned seat and one slack hand visible — the great general reduced to a prop. The chamber has shrunk again: the ceiling beams are visible now, pressing down. The ink-wash background is spare and grey, all warmth drained. A single hanging lamp sways almost imperceptibly. Tsao Tsao's stillness is more frightening than Yuan Shao's urgency.
dialogue: Tsao Tsao: The eunuch evil is of very old standing. But a gaoler would be ample force against it. Why summon armies and increase confusion? Any desire to slay them will speedily become known — and the plan will fail.
Ho Chin: Then, Meng-te — you have some scheme of your own to further.
Tsao Tsao: Ho Chin is the man to throw the empire into confusion.
Ho Chin: Let me think it over.
panels.narration: The Recorder Chen Lin had already set down in ink what every clear eye could see: to summon armies to the capital, to gather bold men into one spot each with his own ambitions, was to turn one's weapons against one's own person — like lighting a furnace to burn a single hair, ruinous force for a trifling act. Now Tsao Tsao made the same argument with fewer words and colder eyes, standing in the grey chamber like a man already calculating what comes after. Ho Chin smiled at them both with the patience of a man who has never yet been proven wrong about himself. Tsao Tsao left without another word, and the lamp swayed once in his wake, and was still.

panels.visual_direction: Tall vertical panel — a full-length rendering of an imperial memorial scroll, held open by two trembling hands at the bottom of frame. The brushwork of the scroll's text is fine and desperate, the characters densely packed. Above it, barely visible in soft focus: Ho Chin's face reading it, expression unchanged, unmoved. The scroll belongs to Chen Lin; his words are rendered as visible calligraphy art within the panel — a visual metaphor for language as plea, as warning, as the last resort of a man without armies. The panel border itself is drawn as if it were a scroll edge, reinforcing the document as physical object. Ink bleeds slightly at the scroll's margins — urgency staining even the paper.
dialogue: Chen Lin (caption from scroll): 'Nay; do not act blindly. The proverb says: to cover the eyes and snatch at swallows is to fool one’s self. Act promptly with the imperial authority already in your hand, and all the Empire will be with you.'

Chen Lin (caption from scroll): 'But summon armies, gather bold men each with his own schemes — and you place yourself in the power of another. Nothing but failure can come of it. Nothing but confusion.'
panels.narration: Chen Lin had set down in careful brushwork what no spoken word had moved Ho Chin to hear: that the eunuchs, for all their malice, were small men — small enough that the authority already in Ho Chin's hands could end them before the lamp burned low, precisely, without chaos. He had urged action prompt and sure, invoking the weight of imperial prestige and the favor of timing. Ho Chin read the memorial, showed it to his partisans, and laid it aside. 'The view of a mere bookworm,' he said, and smiled the smile of a man unequal to the warning he had just received.

panels.visual_direction: Extreme close-up — Ho Chin's face alone, filling the panel. The room behind him is now just shadow. His expression is the most dangerous thing in the scene: serene. There is no doubt in his face, no fear — only the quiet certainty of a man who has never been wrong about himself. His robes fill the lower portion of the frame, elaborate and heavy. One ringed finger touches his jaw in contemplation. The lighting is a single lamp source, one side of his face in warm gold, the other in absolute dark. The artist should render every line of his face with care — this is not a villain's face. It is the face of a man who simply cannot see what is coming.
dialogue: Yuan Shao (off-panel): My lord — at least let us come with you as a guard. Just as a precaution.
Ho Chin: Silly children. What can palace servants do against the man who holds the forces of the Empire in the palm of his hand?
Ho Chin (to himself): Ho Chin is the man they fear. Let them fear him a while longer.
panels.narration: More than half the ministers of state had given up their posts and retired in despair — Lu Chih among them, who had known Tung Cho long and warned plainly that in appearance innocent, he was a very wolf at heart. Ho Chin had sent them all a gracious farewell and summoned the wolf closer still, and mistook the departure of wise men for the withdrawal of the merely timid. He held the forces of the empire, he believed, in the palm of his hand; this was a truth so large it had made him blind to all lesser truths arranged around it. In the lamplight his face was divided — one half bright gold, the other consumed entirely by shadow.

panels.visual_direction: Full-width bird's-eye establishing shot, bleeding off the page's bottom edge — the most expansive panel in the sequence, yet its subject has never been more alone. From directly above, we see Ho Chin as a small, richly-robed figure approaching the massive timber gates of the inner palace, his shadow stretching long across the flagstone courtyard under a flat grey sky. He walks without escort, without armor. The composition is vast and empty around him — the courtyard dwarfs him with deliberate cruelty. The palace walls rise at the top of the frame, rendered in dense ink-wash stone. And there, at the wall's crenellated edge, barely resolved against the grey sky — dark silhouettes. Three. Four. Five figures crouching in stillness, watching the small figure below walk toward them. They are not yet moving. They are waiting. The ink is coldest here: no warm tones, only grey, black, and the pale stone of a sky that offers nothing.
dialogue: Yuan Shao (calling after him): The plot is no longer a secret. Still you may go — if you are ready to fight your way in.
Ho Chin (without turning): What can they do?
panels.narration: At the Chingso Gate the escort was stopped — orders to admit the General and none other — and Ho Chin walked on without pause, as though the stripping away of his guard were a courtesy and not a closing trap. He had been warned by Yuan Shao, by Chen Lin, by Tsao Tsao, by Lu Chih; he had called each of them in turn a bookworm, a timid child, a man unequal to great schemes, and had felt himself confirmed in wisdom by the very consistency of their fear. He walked through the gates alone, beneath a sky the color of old bronze, and did not look up. At the Gate of Abundant Virtue, the two chief eunuchs were waiting, and their followers were already moving to close the circle.

panel_scripts.scene_title: The Assassination of Ho Chin — Head Over the Wall
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Five panels across two pages. Page one: three panels in descending hierarchy — a wide establishing shot at top (full width), then two medium panels side by side below. Page two: two panels — a tall, narrow vertical panel on the left (the arc), and a full bleed splash on the right (Yuan Shao's cry). The vertical panel should feel like a scroll painting; the splash like a war drum struck once. Use heavy ink-wash blacks in panels 3 and 4, then release to stark white sky in the arc panel to create maximum visual shock. Negative space is a weapon here.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE ESTABLISHING SHOT — full page width, cinematic and low-angle. Ho Chin strides through the Gate of Abundant Virtue into a sunlit palace courtyard. His ceremonial robes catch the light — deep crimson and gold, meticulously detailed with dragon embroidery, rendered in rich ink wash. He is shot from slightly below and behind, so he appears enormous against the soaring gate architecture. His head is turned just slightly to show a small, proprietary smile — the expression of a man arriving at a place he believes he owns. The courtyard is unnaturally empty ahead of him. Sunlight pours down in long diagonal shafts. In the extreme background, barely visible in doorway shadows, are still figures — watching, waiting. The architecture frames him like a trap already sprung.
dialogue: Silly children! What can eunuchs do against the man who holds the forces of the Empire in the palm of his hand?
panels.narration: He had been warned — by Ts’ao Ts’ao, by Yuan Shao, by Chʻen Lin who had met him at the very threshold and begged him not to enter. He had dismissed them all as timid men unequal to great schemes. When the eunuchs at the inner gate turned back his escort — the orders were to admit the General and none other — Ho Chin walked on, proudly, into the emptied courtyard. He did not look behind him.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — the courtyard from Ho Chin's perspective, now pulling back to show the geometry of encirclement. Eunuchs emerge from every archway, every doorway, every shadow — not rushing, but stepping forward with the deliberate calm of men who have rehearsed this. Their robes are dark; their faces are expressionless. The gate architecture overhead seems to tilt inward, the pillars converging toward Ho Chin at center. He has stopped walking. His smile is gone. His hand moves toward his sword but the gesture is already too late — it reads as a twitch, not a draw. Use loose, urgent brushwork for the encircling figures; tight, frozen linework for Ho Chin himself. He is the only still thing in the frame.
dialogue: The orders are to admit the General — and none other. Your escort waits outside.
panels.narration: They did not rush. They stepped from every archway, every shadow, every door — dark-robed and deliberate, with the unhurried calm of men who have rehearsed this moment a thousand times in their minds. The eunuchs’ followers quickly closed in around him, and Ho Chin had begun to feel alarmed. His hand moved toward his sword, but found nothing — the gesture of a man who had counted on forces that were no longer here.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP — Chang Jang's face filling almost the entire panel, shot slightly upward as though Ho Chin is looking up at his accuser. Chang Jang's face is extraordinary in its ugliness of expression — not rage, but something colder: twenty years of enforced deference, of bowing and scraping and smiling, compressed into a single moment of release. His eyes are bright. His lips are pulled back. Behind him, barely in frame, dark-robed assassins raise blades. The ink work here should be at its most ferocious — jagged, slashing brushstrokes for Chang Jang's features, deep shadow carving his face into something almost abstract. He looks like a man becoming what he always was.
dialogue: What crime had Tung Tʿai-hou committed that she should die? And when the Mother of the Country was buried — who feigned sickness and did not attend the rites?
We raised you — your paltry, huckstering family — to all the dignity and wealth you have ever known. You would slay us? You call us sordid and dirty — but who, General, is the cleaner?
panels.narration: Chang Jang’s voice rang across the courtyard — not the wheedling tone of a courtier, but something twenty years of bowing and scraping had kept long buried. Ho Chin looked about him for a way to escape, but the eunuchs had closed him in on every side, and then the assassins appeared and did their bloody work. He had held the forces of the Empire in the palm of his hand — and here, at the last, the palm was empty.

panels.visual_direction: VERTICAL NARROW PANEL — tall and thin, like a section cut from a scroll painting. Against an almost pure white sky, a severed head arcs over the top of the palace wall. The head is rendered with unflinching clarity — Ho Chin's face in its last frozen expression, mouth slightly open, topknot trailing. The wall below is just a dark horizontal band of ink at the panel's base. Nothing else. No assassins, no gate, no context — only the arc, the white sky, and the terrible geometry of a life's end. This panel should feel like a single brushstroke. The white space is not emptiness; it is silence.
dialogue: Thy carriage awaits, O General. We are ready to depart.
panels.narration: Yuan Shao had waited long outside the gate, growing impatient at the silence within. At last he had called through the wall: “Thy carriage awaits, O General.” For reply, the head of the murdered officer was flung over the wall. Closing the days of the Hans — the years of their rule were near spent; stupid and tactless was Ho Chin, yet stood he highest in office; many were they who advised him, but he was deaf as he heard not — wherefore fell he a victim under the swords of the eunuchs.

panels.visual_direction: FULL BLEED SPLASH — Yuan Shao below the palace wall, shot wide to show him small against the massive structure yet incandescent with fury. He stands in full armor, one arm extended outward — he has just caught the severed head, or recoiled from it landing at his feet, the blocking deliberately ambiguous. His sword is raised in his other hand, pointing skyward. His face is turned upward and outward toward his soldiers — his mouth open in a full-throated scream. Around him, soldiers are frozen in the first instant before action, their postures coiled. The ink-wash style is at its most atmospheric here: the wall looms dark and textured behind him, the sky above bleeds from ink-gray to white. Yuan Shao is the only thing in sharp focus. Everything else is brushwork and fury.
dialogue: A decree is proclaimed — that Ho Chin contemplated treachery against the throne, and therefore was justly slain! They would have us bow our heads and accept this!
The eunuchs have slain the minister! All who would end this wicked party — TO ME!
panels.narration: A decree was at once proclaimed: Ho Chin had contemplated treachery against the throne, and therefore had been slain; his adherents were pardoned. But Yuan Shao had seen what had been flung over the wall, and all mercy departed from him in that instant. He set one of Ho Chin’s officers to fire the gate, and as the flames took hold, he raised his voice over the roar — a sound that would bring down what remained of the Han dynasty’s long and troubled peace.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Fire in the Palace — The Eunuchs' Last Night
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: Panel 1 is a full-width splash across the top third — the burning gates, monumental and wide. Panels 2 and 3 split the bottom two-thirds vertically, equal width. Page two: Panel 4 is a tall narrow vertical strip on the far left — a gutter panel suggesting a corridor of violence. Panels 5 and 6 share the remaining space, with Panel 5 occupying the upper two-thirds and Panel 6 a wide cinematic strip at the bottom of the page. All panels use ink-wash bleeds with no hard gutters — fire and smoke bleed across borders to unify the chaos. The far right edge of each page carries a thin vertical 'shadow track' showing the Emperor's flight — small figures against total dark, almost like a filmstrip margin.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH ESTABLISHING SHOT. A low, wide angle looking up at the Imperial Palace gates — massive lacquered doors of deep vermillion, now engulfed in roaring columns of orange and black fire. Yuan Shu's armored soldiers pour through the shattered breach like a tide, silhouetted against the inferno. Spears and banners catch the firelight. The architecture above — ornate bracketing, carved ridge beasts — crumbles and falls in embers. Smoke rolls upward into a night sky that has turned the color of blood and ash. The composition echoes a Song Dynasty landscape scroll turned catastrophic: the palace is rendered in precise, reverent linework, and then systematically destroyed by loose, explosive ink-wash strokes of fire. The soldiers are small against the gate's enormity — the building itself is the protagonist of this panel, dying.
panels.narration: The Han dynasty had stood four hundred years, its gates lacquered with the devotion of ten thousand ministers, its pillars held upright by the blood of loyal men and the weight of heaven's mandate. It took one night to end it.
